articles.title: Rochdale Council Generates Nearly £3 Million from Parking Fines Over Three Years
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has collected £2.88 million from parking fines since 2023, with the highest revenue year being 2025. The funds are reinvested into local road infrastructure.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has generated £2.88 million from parking fines over the past three years, according to data obtained through a Freedom of Information request. The figures reveal that the council issued a total of 90,644 parking charge notices (PCNs) from 2023 to 2025, averaging just under £1 million per year. The year 2025 saw the highest revenue, with £990,256 collected from fines.

The total value of the PCNs issued during this period was over £5.6 million, although the actual income is lower due to successful challenges against fines and the costs associated with enforcing them. The council has stated that all revenue from PCNs is reinvested into the local road network, which may include repairs to potholes, road markings, and larger infrastructure projects.

The data also highlights the main hotspots for parking fines in Rochdale, with Newgate, Yorkshire Street Central, and Oldham Road Central being the locations where the highest number of PCNs were issued. The council emphasizes that these fines are not only a source of revenue but are also issued for safety reasons, ensuring that pavements remain accessible for wheelchair users and preventing blind spots at junctions.

This significant revenue from parking fines raises questions about the balance between enforcement and public convenience. Residents may want to consider the implications of these fines on local traffic management and safety. What are your thoughts on the effectiveness of parking enforcement in Rochdale?

articles.title: Power Outage in Newhey Linked to 'Third-Party Interference'
articles.excerpt: Residents in Newhey experienced a power outage lasting approximately three hours following a loud bang linked to third-party interference on the electricity network.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Newhey, Rochdale, were left without power for around three hours following a loud bang associated with an incident on the electricity network. The disruption occurred on the evening of October 18, 2026, and was reported by Electricity North West, who stated that the outage was due to 'third-party interference' on their high-voltage network.

According to a message from Electricity North West, the loud bang was heard at a property on Ogden Lane at the same time the power interruption occurred. While most residents had their power restored by 23:17, one customer remained without supply as further investigations were conducted to ensure safety before restoration could take place.

Electricity North West expressed appreciation for the patience and understanding of the affected residents during the investigation. They confirmed that their teams were working to identify the root cause of the fault and ensure the safety of the network before restoring power to the remaining customer.

Residents are encouraged to stay updated through official channels for any further developments regarding the power supply in their area. For those affected, it is recommended to check the Electricity North West website or contact their customer service for assistance.

articles.title: From air traffic control to author: Ramsbottom retiree supports dementia charity
articles.excerpt: After 36 years working in air traffic control engineering, Ramsbottom resident Ged has published his debut novel Forget Me Not, with profits going to Alzheimer’s Society and around £700 raised so far.
articles.content_html:
After a 36-year career as an engineer working in air traffic control, Ramsbottom resident Ged has found an unexpected new chapter in retirement: becoming a novelist and raising money for people affected by dementia.

His debut novel, Forget Me Not, was released on 3 October 2026. Inspired by real events, the family drama follows Vera, a 91-year-old woman living with dementia, and the relatives whose responses to her illness reveal very different intentions.

At the heart of the story are difficult questions about family loyalty, protection and vulnerability. Some of Vera’s relatives want to keep her safe, while others see an opportunity to take advantage. The novel explores the pressures that dementia can place on families, and what happens when trust is tested.

Ged said the leap from engineering to fiction surprised even him. After spending more than three decades working in air traffic control, he had not expected retirement to lead to the publication of a book.

He has also given the project a charitable purpose. Ged says every penny of profit from Forget Me Not will go to Alzheimer’s Society, and that supporters have already helped raise around £700 since the novel’s release. The total is the author’s reported figure.

To make the story accessible to people who would rather borrow than buy, he has donated copies to libraries in Ramsbottom, Bury, Prestwich and Radcliffe. He hopes the books will be available for local readers to borrow soon.

Forget Me Not is available on Amazon in paperback (£9.99) and Kindle format (£2.99), with access also offered through Kindle Unlimited, according to the author’s announcement. Readers can find it at https://www.amazon.co.uk/dp/B0HJP695NC.

Signed copies can be requested through https://forms.gle/RPyfy2TbDMZZKEUX7, with free hand delivery offered around Bury. Readers can also follow updates about the book at https://www.facebook.com/forgetmenotanovel.

For those whose families have been affected by dementia, Alzheimer’s Society provides information, practical support and advice at https://www.alzheimers.org.uk/.

Ged hopes the novel will both find an audience and make a meaningful contribution to a cause close to many families across Greater Manchester.

articles.title: Overnight Road Closures Planned at Sudden Junction, Rochdale from October 12 to 15
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council will implement overnight road closures around Sudden Junction from October 12 to 15 for resurfacing work, affecting traffic routes and diversions.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that overnight road closures will take place around Sudden Junction from Monday, October 12, to Thursday, October 15. The closures are necessary for resurfacing work, which will include refreshing road markings and renewing traffic signs.

The affected roads will be closed nightly between 8pm and 5am. Manchester Road in Castleton will be closed northbound between Onslow Street and Bolton Road, impacting traffic heading towards Rochdale town centre. Additionally, Silk Street will operate as one-way towards Tesco, preventing drivers from travelling from Tesco towards Manchester Road. Traffic on Bolton Road will also be restricted from turning right onto Manchester Road towards Castleton.

In a statement, the council confirmed that fully signed diversion routes will be in place to guide motorists during the closures. The resurfacing work aims to improve road safety and traffic flow in the area, which has seen increased usage in recent months.

Motorists are advised to plan their journeys accordingly and allow extra time for travel during the closure period. The council will continue to provide updates as the work progresses.

articles.title: Roadworks Scheduled on Well i' th' Lane in Rochdale from 24 October 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced roadworks on Well i' th' Lane starting 24 October 2026, with alternative routes provided for motorists.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks will commence on Well i' th' Lane from 12 midnight on Saturday, 24 October 2026, continuing until 11.59pm on Sunday, 1 November 2026. During this period, part of the road will be temporarily closed to facilitate the necessary works.

Motorists travelling southbound will be diverted via Queen Victoria Street, Oldham Road, and Queensway. The council advises drivers to plan their journeys accordingly to avoid delays during the roadworks.

In addition to Well i' th' Lane, several other roads in the Rochdale area will also undergo maintenance. Notably, Willbutts Lane and Rooley Street will see roadworks starting on 12 October 2026, with closures expected to last for a maximum of 21 days. Willbutts Lane will be closed at the junction with Edenfield Road, extending 14 metres westward, while Rooley Street will be closed at the same junction, extending 10 metres eastward.

Egerton Street in Heywood will also be closed from 12 midnight on Tuesday, 20 October 2026, until 11.59pm on Sunday, 1 November 2026, with the closure beginning at the junction with Hind Hill Street and extending 165 metres westward. Residents and commuters are encouraged to check the Rochdale Borough Council's website for further details, including maps of the affected areas and updates on the roadworks.

articles.title: Castleton night works: Manchester Road’s three traffic phases
articles.excerpt: Overnight restrictions run until 8 November. The council has not published dates for individual phases.
articles.content_html:
Manchester Road drivers face overnight restrictions for Bee Network Phase 2 resurfacing, scheduled from 12 October to 8 November 2026, 8pm–5am. Only one phase operates at a time.

Phase 1 closes Manchester Road between Onslow Street and Bolton Road. Silk Street is westbound-only from Tesco to Manchester Road; right turns from Bolton Road onto Manchester Road are banned.

Phase 2 bans north-eastbound travel on Manchester Road from Bolton Road to Roch Valley Way. There is no left turn from Bolton Road onto Manchester Road. The old Manchester Road section must exit via Roch Valley Way. Manchester Road traffic can only turn left onto Bolton Road. Westbound travel on Silk Street from Tesco to Manchester Road is prohibited.

Phase 3 bans south-westbound travel between Roch Valley Way and Bolton Road. There is no left turn from Edinburgh Way onto Manchester Road, or right turn from Roch Valley Way. Silk Street closes between Manchester Road and Tesco, with no right turn into it from Manchester Road.

Diversions will be signed. Check the current phase before travelling: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/2618/various-roads-roadworks-in-rochdale-from-12-october-2026

articles.title: Heywood councillors vote to end Hopwood Triangle road closure trial
articles.excerpt: Heywood Township councillors have voted unanimously to end the Hopwood Triangle traffic trial after sustained opposition from residents, while the Coronation Avenue HGV parking restriction will remain.
articles.content_html:
Common sense has finally prevailed. At an extraordinary Heywood Township meeting last tonight, councillors voted UNANIMOUSLY to bring the Hopwood Triangle trial on Middleton Road and Magdala Street to an end and remove the road closures. The restriction preventing heavy wagons from parking on Coronation Avenue will remain in place, helping to protect local streets.

For residents, this decision has been a long time coming. The consultation results could hardly have been clearer: 86% of the approximately 700 respondents opposed the scheme. Yet despite that overwhelming response, the trial was approved and went ahead. Residents subsequently raised serious concerns about congestion, access, road safety and the effect on local businesses. People living on Manchester Road also felt they had been left out of the original consultation despite subsequently experiencing the impact of displaced traffic. The timing was another major concern. The trial began during the quieter summer holiday period, with residents warning that the true impact would become much more apparent once schools reopened and normal traffic levels returned. Last night, local people turned out in numbers to make sure their voices were heard. More than 50 residents attended the extraordinary meeting, but the size of the room at the old Police Station quickly became an issue. With residents understandably frustrated about access to a public meeting concerning their own streets, tensions rose and the meeting came close to being suspended. At that point, Reform UK Councillor Stuart Crawford intervened constructively. Recognising that many residents had already heard the Highways presentations and wanted councillors to make a decision, Stuart engaged directly with those in attendance, helped calm the situation and pressed for the meeting to move on to the vote rather than risk the evening ending without a decision. The vote was then taken. Every councillor voted to end the trial. That means the temporary road closures will now be removed, while the restriction on heavy wagons parking on Coronation Avenue will remain. And then there is the cost. The figures presented for the scheme are stark: £110,000 to install the temporary measures. That is £110,000 of public money associated with introducing and then removing a trial which had already been rejected by 86% of consultation respondents. The scheme was voted through back in November by Labour councillors Angela Brown, Paul O’Neil, Peter Hodgkinson, Peter Joinson, Susan Emmott and Liam O’Rourke, despite 86% of consultation respondents opposing it. Last night, the decision went the other way. Whatever political arguments follow, one fact should not be forgotten: local residents spoke up, kept speaking up and ultimately got the result they had been asking for. Reform UK will continue to stand with residents when decisions affecting their communities need to be challenged. A huge thank you to everybody who attended, everybody who responded to the original consultation, and everybody who refused to allow their concerns to be ignored. This was people power in action, and people power won.

articles.title: Edenfield Road reopens early after resurfacing work completed ahead of schedule
articles.excerpt: Edenfield Road between the White Lion and Nutters has reopened early after contractors completed resurfacing and lining work ahead of schedule.
articles.content_html:
Edenfield Road between the White Lion and Nutters has reopened to traffic after resurfacing works were completed ahead of schedule.

Norden councillor Paul Ellison MBE confirmed on Saturday that the road is now open and that the road closure which had been expected on Sunday will no longer be required.

Contractors completed the main resurfacing work early, with Saturday seeing the final road-lining work carried out. Cat's-eye road studs are due to be fitted on Monday, but the road itself has reopened.

Councillor Ellison thanked Rochdale Borough Council, A&T Surfacing and Rhodes & Son Construction for completing the scheme ahead of schedule, describing the finished work as a fantastic job.

The reopening will be welcome news for residents and motorists using one of the principal routes through Norden. The works had required traffic restrictions while the carriageway was resurfaced, with further closure time originally expected over the weekend.

With the contractors finishing earlier than planned, drivers can now use the stretch between the White Lion and Nutters without the anticipated Sunday closure.

Motorists should remain aware that the final cat's-eye inserts are expected to be fitted on Monday and should follow any temporary traffic management in place while that work is completed.

articles.title: Residents voice concerns over dangerous driving and alleged street racing on Milkstone Road
articles.excerpt: Residents have raised concerns about dangerous driving and alleged street racing on Milkstone Road, with calls for stronger enforcement to improve road safety.
articles.content_html:
Residents and business owners along Milkstone Road are continuing to raise concerns about dangerous driving, excessive speeding and alleged late-night street racing, with many calling for stronger enforcement before someone is seriously injured.

Milkstone Road is one of Rochdale's busiest routes, carrying thousands of vehicles each day while also serving local shops, schools, places of worship and residential streets. For many residents, the road should be a safe route for families, pedestrians and cyclists. However, some say that during evenings and late at night, it can become the scene of drivers accelerating aggressively, revving engines and travelling at excessive speeds.

While there is no evidence to suggest organised street racing is a regular occurrence, residents have reported vehicles appearing to race one another, performing rapid acceleration and driving in a manner they believe is dangerous. Such behaviour can create significant risks for other motorists, pedestrians and nearby residents, particularly on a road with numerous junctions, crossings and side streets.

The concerns reflect a wider national problem. Police forces across the country have stepped up action against illegal street racing and antisocial driving, warning that the behaviour can have devastating consequences. The Government has also strengthened powers allowing police to seize and destroy vehicles used in antisocial driving offences in appropriate circumstances.

Road safety already forms one of the priorities for Greater Manchester Police's Milkstone and Deeplish neighbourhood team. Officers say they are carrying out high-visibility traffic operations, speed enforcement and action against inconsiderate motorists alongside wider work tackling antisocial behaviour and organised crime in the area.

Residents say the issue extends beyond noise. High-speed driving can intimidate pedestrians, discourage people from walking to local businesses and increase the risk of collisions. Milkstone Road is a busy mixed-use corridor where children, elderly residents and shoppers regularly cross the road throughout the day.

National road safety experts have consistently warned that excessive speed dramatically reduces the time available for drivers to react while increasing both the likelihood and severity of collisions. Even where no crash occurs, repeated antisocial driving can have a lasting impact on neighbourhoods through noise, fear and disruption.

Many local residents are now calling for additional measures, including increased police patrols during evening hours, more targeted traffic enforcement, mobile speed checks and continued action against drivers found to be driving dangerously or inconsiderately.

Greater Manchester Police encourages anyone witnessing dangerous driving to report it where it is safe to do so. Dashcam footage, CCTV and details such as registration numbers, locations and times can all assist officers in identifying offenders. Residents should always call 999 if they believe there is an immediate danger to life or serious risk to road users.

For most drivers, Milkstone Road is simply another journey home or to work. However, residents hope that continued enforcement and responsible driving will ensure the road remains safe for everyone who lives, works and travels through one of Rochdale's busiest neighbourhoods.
